PFAS stands for Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances, which is a large group of human-made chemicals that have been in use since the 1940s. These substances are known for their unique properties, such as resistance to heat, water, and oil. Due to these characteristics, PFAS have been widely used in various industries, including manufacturing, food packaging, and firefighting foams.

PFAS are often referred to as "forever chemicals" because they do not break down easily in the environment and can persist for a very long time. This persistence means that PFAS can accumulate in the environment and in living organisms, including humans, leading to potential health risks.

There are thousands of different types of PFAS, but two of the most well-known and studied are perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). These chemicals have been linked to various health issues, including liver damage, thyroid disease, immune system problems, and cancer.

Due to growing concerns about the health and environmental impacts of PFAS, there has been increased regulation and research into these substances. Many countries and states are implementing stricter regulations on the use and disposal of PFAS, and there is ongoing research into safer alternatives to these chemicals.
